entities.name: Aurelius Victor
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Sextus Aurelius Victor, born around 320 CE in Africa, was a distinguished Roman historian and politician whose concise Latin historical works provide invaluable insights into the reigns of Roman emperors from Augustus to Constantius II. His literary output, particularly the *Caesares*, served as a critical source for understanding the shifting political landscape and imperial succession during the tumultuous third and fourth centuries of the Roman Empire, bridging the gap between earlier classical historians and later Byzantine chroniclers. Elevated to the office of *praefectus urbi* of Rome in 389 CE, Victor exemplified the intellectual elite who navigated the complex administrative and cultural currents of a declining yet still powerful Western Roman Empire.

Victor's primary contribution to historical scholarship lies in his *Liber de Caesaribus*, a series of biographical sketches of Roman emperors and prominent figures from Augustus (27 BCE) to Constantius II (361 CE). This work, likely completed around 361 CE, is characterized by its succinct style and focus on moral lessons derived from imperial actions. He is also credited with three other related works: *Origo Gentis Romanae*, detailing Rome's origins; *De Viris Illustribus Urbis Romae*, a collection of biographies of famous Romans; and *Epitome de Caesaribus*, a compressed version of the *Liber de Caesaribus*. While the authorship of the latter three is debated, they are often grouped together as the *Historia Tripartita* or *Corpus Aurelianum*, reflecting a cohesive historical project.
